a_intro.text: In just twelve years, the glow of towns and cities has spread across the planet, tracing where people live and build.
Listen as the light grows and the notes climb.

a_hearing.text: Listen to the planet after dark.
NASA satellites photographed Earth's lights at night, every year from 2012 to 2023.
We divided each image into eight regions, and gave each region a voice.
As a region glows brighter, its note climbs higher.
The brighter the lights, the louder it sings.
The chorus of a world that never sleeps.

a_visual.text: This is our world at night, seen from orbit.
Every point of light is a city, a highway, a harbour.
A place where people live and work.
From 2012 to 2023, the image moves forward one year at a time, in step with the music.
Watch the lights spread, and listen to them grow.

b_intro.text: Behind that growing glow is a rising demand for energy.
As greenhouse gases build up, the planet warms.
Listen to a hundred and forty-four years of changing temperature, from pole to pole.

b_hearing.text: For a hundred and forty-four years, scientists have taken the planet's temperature.
Here, eight bands of latitude, from the Arctic to Antarctica, each play a single note.
The warmer a band becomes, the lower its note falls.
Beneath them, a heartbeat quickens as the whole world warms.
And slowly, the harmony begins to fall apart.
This is the sound of a warming planet.

b_visual.text: This is NASA's temperature record, from 1880 to 2023, divided into eight bands from pole to pole.
Each row is a band of the Earth, and each mark is a year, placed by how much warmer or cooler it was than the average from 1951 to 1980.
As the decades pass, the newest marks glow red and creep to the right.
By 2023, the Arctic, on the top row, has warmed the most of all.

c_intro.text: Yet the living land fights back, breathing in our carbon every summer.
But when drought takes hold, as it did in 2015 and 2016, its breath begins to falter.

c_hearing.text: In the northern summer, forests and fields draw carbon dioxide from the air.
In winter, they let it go.
Here, strings follow that breath, month by month, from 2003 to 2017.
A solo violin climbs as the land breathes in.
Cellos and racing violins swell as it breathes out.
Each January, a timpani strikes, louder in the years the land absorbed less.
Listen for 2016 and 2017, when the breath falters.

c_visual.text: This is NASA's map of the living land.
Green marks places absorbing carbon dioxide.
Month by month, the colours follow the seasons.
Green sweeps across the north every summer, and fades each winter.
In 2015 and 2016, watch the Amazon turn magenta, as a severe drought grips the rainforest.
